1.definition: The last strong ruler of the Rouran, the steppe empire the Göktürks served as ironworking vassals. When Anagui treated the Türk leader Bumin with contempt, Bumin revolted, smashed the Rouran in 552, and founded the Türk Khaganate in their place — making Anagui the man whose arrogance handed the steppe to the Turks.

The Chinese imperial bride Bumin secured from the Western Wei court in 551. Marrying a Chinese princess gave a steppe ruler semi-imperial standing by Chinese diplomatic convention; no individual record of this particular princess survives.

4.definition: A Sogdian merchant who became the Türk empire's chief diplomat in the 560s, leading missions across Persia and on to Byzantium to open up the silk trade — the human face of the Sogdian network that ran the khaganate's commerce.
The last king of the Hephthalite Empire, defeated and killed around 560 CE when the Türks and Sasanian Persians crushed the Hephthalites in a coordinated two-front war.
The flat lowland of the Pannonian (Carpathian) Basin in central Europe, around modern Hungary — where the Avars built their khaganate in the late sixth century after fleeing west.

5.definition: A son of Ishbara Qaghan and an eastern Türk claimant during the succession wars of the 580s. The Sui court backed him against the rival Apa faction as part of its strategy of keeping the Türks fighting each other.

6.definition: A Türk nobleman who in 679 led the first major revolt against Tang Chinese rule, the opening move in the Türks' fight to win back their independence.

7.definition: One of the Turkic-speaking steppe tribes of the northern Mongolian frontier. They were among the peoples the Türk ruler Kapaghan subdued in the 690s while expanding his power.

7.definition: A Türk leader of the Ashide clan whose 679 revolt against Tang overlordship was crushed by the general Pei Xingjian. His rising was a dress rehearsal for the successful Kutlugh revolt three years later.
Spanning the connected landmass of Europe and Asia. Used here for the trade-and-tribute web that linked the Türk court to China, Sogdia, and beyond.
The armies of the early Islamic caliphate, mostly Arabian in origin, whose conquests in the early 700s swept from Spain to Central Asia and pressed Constantinople in the great siege of 717–718.

The settled Chinese model of running a state: a salaried bureaucracy of appointed officials, written law codes, fixed capitals, tax registers, and administration by paperwork. Tonyukuk argued that adopting it would dissolve the mobility and military edge that made the steppe Türks strong — so the Türks should take what they needed from China by trade and tribute without governing like China.

8.definition: The Uyghur leader who in 744 finished off the collapsing Second Turk Khaganate, took the imperial title for himself, and founded the Uyghur Khaganate — the new steppe power that replaced the Göktürks (no relation to the earlier Bilge Kagan despite the shared name).

The Uyghur khagan (reigned 759-779) who converted his empire to Manichaeism in 762 after Sogdian missionaries introduced him to the faith during his occupation of the Tang capital. His choice made the Uyghurs the only steppe empire ever to adopt Manichaeism as a state religion.

The Türk-speaking nomads who poured into Anatolia after the Seljuk victory at Manzikert (1071), gradually converting the peninsula from Greek-speaking Christianity to Türk-speaking Islam over the following centuries and forming the ancestral core of the later Ottoman and modern Turkish populations.
